title: Q4 planning

calendarEvent.title: Q4 planning
calendarEvent.description:
Q4 planning (90 min). Aisha facilitates, Shreyas co-runs.

Agenda:
1. Q3 retro: what went well / what didn't (15 min)
2. Candidate Q4 bets + rough sizing in engineer-weeks
3. Debate
4. Decisions
5. Owners, dates, milestones, risks and dependencies
6. Hiring (board meeting is Tue 29 Sept)
7. Wrap-up

Pre-read and candidate list: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Xq4PlnDeIno7rTz2026Q4bets/edit
Please add your sizing comments to the doc before the meeting.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, I think we're recording. Hi everyone, give it a minute, people are still trickling in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Hi hi. Shreyas, are you in the office or at home today?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Office. It's weirdly empty, I've got the whole big table to myself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Living the dream. I'm at home, the dog has been fed so we should be safe for at least an hour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Hey all, hi everyone.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Hey Maya. How are you holding up?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Um, honestly, tired. But fine. I got about six hours last night which is an improvement.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We'll get to that, I want to talk about the incident properly in the retro part. Hi Diego.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Hey, hello. Sorry, I was fighting with a Bluetooth headset, it decided it wanted to pair with my laptop and my phone at the same time.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Hi everyone. I'm here, I'm going to keep my camera off for a sec, I'm just finishing a sandwich.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Totally fine, Noor. Priya, are you there? I see your tile but it's frozen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: I'm here. Can you hear me? My video seems to be stuck but the audio should be okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Audio's good, don't worry. Tom, are you with us?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Yeah, I'm here, I'm here. Can you hear, uh, can you hear me?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tom, you're cutting out pretty badly. We got about every third word.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Is that better? I switched off the VPN.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Much better, yeah. Loud and clear now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Okay, sorry. The support VPN does something horrible to Meet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No worries. So we're missing Lena, she messaged me that her call with the Midwest prospect is running over, she'll be about ten minutes late. Let's just start, she knows the agenda.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Welcome to Q4 planning. This is the big one, ninety minutes, so please, if you need a break, there's going to be a five-minute break around the middle.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Shreyas and I are running this together. I'm going to do the business side and facilitate, and Shreyas is going to own the capacity numbers and the engineering sizing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yep. And I'll be the one saying no a lot, apologies in advance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's literally your job today. So the agenda, it's in the doc linked from the invite. First, a quick Q3 retro, what went well and what didn't, maybe fifteen minutes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Second, the candidate bets for Q4, with rough sizing in engineer-weeks. There are seven of them on the list. Third, we debate, because we obviously can't do seven things.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Fourth, decisions. Fifth, owners, dates, milestones, risks. Sixth, hiring, because the board meeting is tomorrow and I need to know what I'm asking for.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And then a wrap-up.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Seven things in one quarter, that's ambitious.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Seven things is not happening, Diego, don't worry.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Right. So, retro. I'll go first with the numbers and then I want to hear from everyone, not just the people who like talking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Q3 closed really well, honestly better than I expected in July. We ended the quarter at forty-one paying customers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: ARR is two point four million, up from one point nine at the end of Q2. So that's roughly twenty-six percent growth in a quarter, which, I mean, I'll take that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: That's amazing. Was that mostly new logos or expansion?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Both, which is the nice part. Net revenue retention is a hundred and eighteen percent, so existing customers are adding technicians. Fernhollow added twelve seats in August, before, you know, everything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Gross margin is at seventy-eight percent. Burn is around three hundred and ten thousand a month and we have five point nine million in the bank. So roughly nineteen months of runway.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Which, for the engineering folks, means we are not in a panic, but we also don't have the luxury of doing seven things badly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Exactly. What I'll say to the board tomorrow is that the business is healthy and the main risk is execution, not cash.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Can I ask about the enterprise tier? How many of the forty-one are on the sixty-dollar tier with SSO?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Six. Six of the forty-one are on enterprise. Everyone else is on the forty-five dollar per technician plan.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Okay, that's more than I thought. That matters for the SOC 2 conversation later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It does. Okay, so what went well beyond the numbers. Let's go around.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Maya, you want to start, or do you want to go last?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'll go. Um, I think the thing that went well for me was the Microsoft 365 connector. We shipped it in July and it's been, knock on wood, really stable.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fourteen customers are using it now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And that was the thing everyone said would be a nightmare.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: It was a nightmare to build. It's not a nightmare to run, which is what matters.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Diego, what about you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: For me, the dispatch board redesign. The drag and drop on the board, that landed well. Dispatchers are actually using the keyboard shortcuts, which I didn't expect at all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Can I add to that? In the usability sessions, the time to reassign a job went from something like forty seconds to under fifteen. That's my favourite number of the quarter.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Noor gets the credit for that, I just built what she drew.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: That is not true, but thank you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Priya, how about infra?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Infrastructure-wise, we moved the job queue off the old Redis box onto the managed service and we had zero downtime during the migration. And we got SOC 2 Type I done in August.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Which I want to call out, because Type I was a lot of policy writing that nobody else wanted to do.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Nobody wanted to do it, including me. But it's done.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Tom, how was the support side?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Uh, yeah. So first response time went down, we're averaging about two hours during business hours, down from like five in Q2. The macros and the new help centre articles helped a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: The other good thing is we started tagging tickets properly, so I can actually tell you what people complain about now, instead of guessing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: That's going to be useful in about twenty minutes, so hold that thought.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Will do, it's all tagged.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Noor, anything else from you?

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Mostly the research program. We did eleven customer interviews in Q3, which is more than all of last year. And a lot of what I heard is about onboarding, which, again, we'll get to.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Great. And from me, I'll just say sales. Lena closed nine new logos this quarter, which is a record.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: She's not here to hear it, so somebody tell her I said it nicely.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'll put it in the notes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, so what didn't go well. And I want to be honest here, this is not a blame thing. The big one is obviously Calendar Sync one point four.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yeah, I know it is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Maya, do you want to walk through it, or would you prefer Shreyas does it? Either is fine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: No, I'll do it, it's fine. So, Calendar Sync v1.4 shipped on the fifteenth of September.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Hi, hi, sorry, sorry. I'm here. Sorry everyone, I'm about ten minutes late, my call with the facilities management prospect ran over and I couldn't get off.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No problem, Lena, welcome. We're in the retro. We just did the good stuff, and I said very nice things about you, which you missed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Of course I did. Can someone repeat them? Slowly?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Nine new logos, a record. That's the summary.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: I'll take it. Okay, sorry Maya, I cut you off. Oh wait, one quick thing, I wanted to check a number before I forget, because the prospect asked me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Our ARR is two point six now, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Two point four. Two point six was the stretch target we had in the plan, we didn't hit that one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Two point four. Okay, good, I didn't say a number on the call, I just said we were growing fast. Phew.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Two point four million, up from one point nine. Forty-one customers. That's what you can say.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Got it. Sorry Maya, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. So, v1.4 shipped on the fifteenth of September. The change was meant to improve how we handle recurring events, because before that we were missing some updates to recurring series.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And what we didn't catch is the case where a technician has a recurring event in Google Calendar, and one single occurrence of that series gets moved. Like a weekly meeting that gets shifted from Tuesday to Wednesday just once.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: When that happens, Google gives us the moved occurrence as a separate event with the same iCalUID but with a recurrence ID. And our code treated it as a brand new event. So we created a duplicate job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And then every poll it created another one?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Not every poll, thankfully, but every time the occurrence changed at all. So if someone edited it twice, you got two extra jobs. It compounded.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the customer impact.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fernhollow got hit hardest by far, because a lot of their technicians use recurring events for their standing maintenance visits. About a hundred and thirty duplicate jobs over roughly two weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: And their dispatchers didn't realise at first, so some technicians actually drove out to jobs that were duplicates. Owen was, um, not happy. He was polite about it, but not happy.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Which is fair. If my technicians were driving to phantom jobs I'd be furious too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Where are we on the fix?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We have a mitigation in place since Friday, so no new duplicates are being created, we're filtering moved occurrences out on ingest. But that's a band-aid. The proper fix is to dedupe on the iCalUID plus the recurrence ID.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And then a cleanup script that finds the existing duplicates and merges them without breaking any jobs that were already assigned or completed. That's the scary part.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: When do you think the real fix lands?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'm aiming for next week. Probably early October. I don't want to rush the cleanup script, because if it merges the wrong jobs we have a second incident.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Agreed. Please don't rush it. A week late is way better than a cleanup script that eats real jobs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: I can review the cleanup script, by the way. I'd like a dry-run mode that just outputs what it would merge, and we send that list to Owen before we run it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes, that's exactly what I was planning. Dry run first, Tom shares it with Fernhollow, then we run it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Happy to do that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. So the thing I want us to learn from this, not just the fix. Shreyas, you had some thoughts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah. A few things. One, we didn't have test fixtures for recurring events with exceptions.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We had recurring events, we had single events, but not the exception case. That's on me, I reviewed the PR.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Two, we shipped v1.4 to all customers at once. No staged rollout. If we'd gone to five customers for a week first, we'd have caught it with maybe ten duplicates instead of a hundred and thirty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And three, Maya ended up on call for basically the whole incident, for almost two weeks, because she's the only one who really knows the sync code. That's a bus factor problem and it's also just not fair to Maya.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I mean, I didn't mind, it's my code.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's our code. And you look exhausted, I'm just saying it out loud.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Fair. I am exhausted.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: On the staged rollout point, do we have a way to do that today? Like, per-customer feature flags on the sync service?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Not really. We have flags in the web app, but the sync workers just run one version for everyone. That's something v2 has to fix from day one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: I'd add that the staged rollout should be the default for anything touching customer data. Not just sync. Imports, the mobile app, all of it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Agreed. I'd like v2 to have per-customer rollout built in, so we can move five customers, watch for a week, then move the next batch.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's already in my head for the design. Beta cohort first, then batches, with polling still running underneath as a safety net until we're confident.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And the test fixtures? Is that fixed now?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Partly. I added fixtures for moved occurrences and cancelled occurrences last week, while I was debugging. There are probably more edge cases, like all-day events across time zones, but the worst one is covered.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Good. I'd like the postmortem to list the edge cases we know we're not covering yet, even if we don't fix them all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yeah, I'll put a known-gaps section in it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Maya, are you going to write up the postmortem? I know you've got notes all over Slack.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yeah. I'll publish the v1.4 postmortem by Thursday. The draft is mostly written, I just need to add the timeline and the action items.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Thursday the first. Great. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Can I ask something maybe naive? Should we tell all customers about it, or just the affected ones?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We've told the affected ones directly. There were four customers with duplicates, Fernhollow was by far the biggest. I don't think we need a broad announcement, but it does connect to the status page idea later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Okay, that makes sense to me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The second thing that didn't go well is the mobile release. Diego?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Yeah. So the mobile app version three point two was supposed to go out mid August, and it actually went out on the... it was the third of September?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: No, sorry, the fourth. The fourth of September. So about three weeks late.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What were the main causes, in your view?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Honestly, two things. One, we got rejected by App Store review twice.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Once for a location permission string that was too vague, and once because the demo account we gave them had expired. Which, embarrassing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And two, the scope kept growing. We added the photo attachments thing halfway through because a customer asked for it, and it touched a lot of code.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: That one's on me, I promised photo attachments to a prospect.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It's fine, they did sign, so.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: They did sign. Fourteen technicians. You're welcome.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, so lessons there. I'm hearing, build App Store review time into every mobile date, and freeze scope once a release is in progress.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Yes. I'd say for planning purposes, assume a week for App Store review. It's usually a day or two, but the bad cases are what kill you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let's carry that into the offline mode conversation, because that's a mobile release too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Anything else that didn't go well? Be honest.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Can I say one? The support load during the incident was huge, and I was basically doing it alone. I think I answered something like sixty tickets about duplicates in a week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: I don't want to complain, but it was a lot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: No, that's a really fair point, Tom. And it's part of why I want the capacity numbers to include support time this quarter.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, my capacity math includes a support rotation, actually. Engineers help Tom for a few hours a week. We'll see it on the slide.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: One more from me. We still don't have a proper way to tell customers when something's broken. During the incident, people found out from their dispatchers, not from us.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: That's the status page thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Right. It's on the candidates list. Okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Good retro, everyone. Thank you, especially Maya.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Thanks, I appreciate that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: One last thing on the retro, and then we move on. I want to propose that we don't ship any more feature changes to Calendar Sync v1 in Q4. Bug fixes only.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: All new sync work goes into v2.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Strongly agree. v1 is polling-based and it's held together with tape at this point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes please. Every time we touch v1 something else moves.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Anyone against? Okay. So that's a decision.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Calendar Sync v1 is bug-fix only for Q4.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Does that mean I can't promise anyone sync improvements this quarter?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: You can promise them v2. Which, if this meeting goes the way I think it will, is coming in December.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Okay, that's good enough for me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay. Moving to the candidate bets. Shreyas, over to you.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Great. Give me a sec, I'm going to share my screen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, can you see my screen? It should be a spreadsheet with a big orange row at the top.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I see a spreadsheet. I don't see orange, I see, um, a sort of salmon colour.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's orange on my monitor. Anyway. Can everyone see it?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Priya, is your frozen video affecting your screen share view?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: No, I can see it fine. It's just me that's frozen. Very flattering frozen face, too.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay. So before we talk about what we want, I want to talk about what we have. This is the capacity for Q4, in engineer-weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We have six engineers, if you count me at half time, which is generous, because I'm also doing hiring and board stuff. So call it five and a half people.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Q4 is thirteen weeks. Five and a half times thirteen is about seventy engineer-weeks gross.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That sounds like a lot when you say it like that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It does, and then reality happens. On-call takes one person full time every week. That's thirteen engineer-weeks gone right away.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The support rotation, engineers helping Tom with escalations, I've estimated at about eight engineer-weeks over the quarter. Tom, does that feel right after September?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: After September, honestly it feels low. But September was abnormal. In a normal month, yeah, eight for the quarter is probably okay.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, I'll keep eight and we'll watch it. Then holidays.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thanksgiving week for the US folks, the last two weeks of December where realistically nobody's shipping anything, plus people's personal time off. I've put ten.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And then interviewing. If the board approves the two roles, we're going to be doing a lot of interviews. I've put five engineer-weeks for that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So seventy minus thirteen, minus eight, minus ten, minus five. That's thirty-four. And I'm holding back four as buffer, because something will go wrong, it always does.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So the number I want everyone to have in their head is thirty. We have about thirty engineer-weeks available in Q4, after on-call and support and everything else.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Thirty. Everyone got that? Thirty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Is that thirty per person or thirty total?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Thirty total. For the whole team.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Oh. Okay. That's, um, that's smaller than I was hoping.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah. It's smaller than I was hoping too. Okay, now the candidates.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'm going to go down the list and give the rough sizing. These are rough, plus or minus thirty percent, please don't quote them to customers.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: First, Calendar Sync v2. This is moving from five-minute polling to webhook push for both Google and Microsoft. Maya and I sized it at eleven engineer-weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Ten to twelve, really. Eleven is the middle. The Google side is maybe four, the Microsoft side is more like five because of the Graph subscription stuff, and then two for migration and rollout.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Second, SOC 2 Type II. Priya, you want to explain the number?

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: Sure. So Type II isn't a project in the normal sense. The auditor observes our controls over a window, usually three to six months.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: We want the window to start on the first of November.

segments.speaker: Speaker 6
segments.text: The engineering cost is in getting controls actually operating before the window starts, things like access reviews, change management evidence, logging, vendor reviews. And then keeping them running. I've estimated six engineer-weeks total, most of it mine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Third, mobile offline mode. Diego.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: So full offline mode, meaning technicians can view their jobs, edit them, add notes and photos, complete jobs, all without signal, and it syncs back when they reconnect. That's about ten engineer-weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: The hard part is conflict resolution. If a dispatcher reassigns a job while the technician is offline and the technician completes it, what wins? That's where most of the time goes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fourth, onboarding revamp. Noor, Tom.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: So this is the new-customer onboarding flow. Right now getting a new customer live takes on average, Tom, what was it, nineteen days?

segments.speaker: Speaker 7
segments.text: Nineteen days median from contract signed to first job dispatched. Some take over a month.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: And most of that is CSV imports failing, calendar connection confusion, and people not knowing how to set up their technicians' skills and regions. The engineering part is about six engineer-weeks. Plus my design time, which isn't in that number.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fifth, route optimisation. This is the feature where we suggest the order of jobs for a technician's day to minimise driving. I've put twelve engineer-weeks, and honestly that might be optimistic.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It's definitely optimistic. Twelve is if we use an off-the-shelf solver and don't do anything clever.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Sixth, the Salesforce integration. Syncing accounts, contacts, and work orders between Salesforce and Deino. Eight engineer-weeks.

segments.speaker: Speaker 8
segments.text: Eight? I thought it was more like three. It's just an integration, we read the accounts and push the jobs, right?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: If it was one-way, read only, maybe three or four. But the two deals you mentioned want it bi-directional. Work order status flowing back into Salesforce, custom fields, the whole thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Bi-directional sync is where the time goes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
